speaker: Scott Kirby
title: Scott Kirby - United Airlines CEO
question: Why do major airlines mostly stock indulgent snacks on flights despite passengers asking for healthier food?
guest: The truth is, on airplanes, what people say they want and what they actually pick is different. Hardly anyone takes the healthy options. So we go with what consumers actually want, and we just use the data of what consumers want to make the picks. People tell you that they want healthy, but they get on airplanes for whatever reason, and healthy is low on the list of things that they actually select. Watch the snack basket when it goes around. I take bananas, because I like bananas and I do actually like to eat healthy, and almost every time I take a banana, the flight attendant makes a comment, "Wow, nobody takes the banana," because there's all this junk food in there, and that's what gets taken.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because what passengers say they want and what they actually buy and eat are different things, and airlines stock to the latter.

Surveys show travelers asking for healthier options, but sales data consistently favor chips, cookies, candy and alcohol. Flying nudges people toward indulgence: they are stressed, bored, tired, or in a "treat yourself" travel mindset. Cabin conditions also work against lighter food, since low humidity, low pressure and engine noise dull the perception of sweet and salty flavors, so strongly seasoned, sugary, or salty snacks simply taste better at altitude.

Economics and logistics reinforce this. Packaged indulgent snacks are cheap, shelf-stable, lightweight, compact, and need no refrigeration, while fresh items such as fruit, salads and yogurt spoil quickly, require cold storage in very limited galley space, and generate costly waste when they go unsold. Airlines that have trialed healthier items often saw them sell poorly and get cut.

So the result is a rational response to revealed preferences and operating constraints: a token healthy option or two, with the bulk of the cart given to what reliably sells.

This is from general knowledge; I did not run a search.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Major airlines stock mostly indulgent snacks because actual passenger behavior, catering economics, and cabin physics all favor sweet and salty comfort foods over nutritious alternatives.

First, there is a wide gap between stated and revealed preferences: flyers routinely ask for healthier options in surveys, yet onboard consumption and sales data show that stressed or vacation-minded travelers overwhelmingly pick cookies, chips, and pretzels—and complain loudly when favorites like Biscoff are cut—leaving healthier items uneaten and wasted. Logistics and cost reinforce this pattern. Mass-produced refined snacks cost pennies per serving, require no refrigeration, survive multi-leg turnarounds in cramped galleys without spoiling, and easily avoid common allergens like nuts, whereas fresh or minimally processed alternatives are far pricier and more perishable. Finally, flying alters taste perception: dry, low-pressure cabin air and loud engine noise dull sensitivity to sweet and salty flavors, making bold, sugar- and salt-forward treats taste satisfying at cruising altitude while subtler healthy foods often taste flat.

noweb.answer: Airlines stock indulgent snacks primarily because of a stark gap between what passengers say and what they actually do, reinforced by cabin biology and logistics. Although flyers routinely request healthier options on surveys, onboard data consistently show that travelers choose cookies, chips, and pretzels in the moment, often treating flights as an excuse to indulge or seeking comfort during stressful travel. Physiology plays a major role as well: low cabin pressure and dry air dull human taste buds and sense of smell, reducing sensitivity to sweet and salty flavors by roughly thirty percent and leaving mildly seasoned healthy foods tasting bland. Finally, airline economics and operations heavily favor processed snacks. Shelf-stable items are inexpensive, require no refrigeration, occupy minimal galley space, weigh very little, and survive flight delays across multiple routes without spoiling, whereas fresh, perishable alternatives cost far more to source and generate significant waste when left uneaten.

Mostly because what passengers say they want differs from what they actually buy. In surveys, travelers ask for fresh fruit, salads and protein options. Airline sales data keep showing that chips, cookies, candy and cheese-and-cracker boxes sell best, partly because many people see a flight as a time to treat themselves. When carriers have tested healthier menus, more of that food often went unsold and was thrown out.

Logistics push the same way. Galleys have little refrigeration and space, and every pound adds fuel cost. Catering has to be loaded hours before departure and survive delays, so packaged snacks with a long shelf life are cheaper, safer and less wasteful than perishable fresh food. Uniform packaged items also scale easily across thousands of daily flights.

Taste plays a role too. Dry cabin air and low pressure dull our sense of salt and sweetness by roughly a third, so strongly flavored salty or sugary foods taste better at altitude. Finally, branded treats such as Biscoff cookies or stroopwafels work as cheap, memorable marketing. Some airlines now offer a few healthier items, usually in premium cabins or for purchase.

noweb.answer:
Airlines rely on indulgent snacks largely because passenger behavior at 35,000 feet rarely matches what people say in surveys. While travelers often ask for healthier options, once onboard—stressed, fatigued, or in a treat-yourself mindset—they overwhelmingly reach for salty, sweet comfort foods. Cabin physics reinforces this: low air pressure and dry air dull our sense of smell and taste, muting subtle, fresh flavors while making heavily seasoned, crunchy, or sugary snacks far more satisfying.

Operational economics seal the deal. Fresh, healthy foods are expensive, heavy, bulky, and perishable. They require refrigeration in tight galleys, add weight that increases fuel burn, and create costly waste when flights are delayed or items go unsold. By contrast, packaged snacks like pretzels, cookies, and chips are lightweight, inexpensive in bulk, and shelf-stable across multiple flight legs. Because airlines operate on thin margins and limited storage, they prioritize items that are cheap to carry, won't spoil, and reliably get eaten.
